judge_assessment.explanation: The ACCEPT holds. I recomputed every value independently: 320 thousand and r = 0.25; b = 1.5 from 240b^3 = 810; t = 4 from 1.5^t = 5.0625; ln 1.5 = 0.405465 -> 0.405; 1 - 0.85 = 0.15 and 80(0.85)^4 = 41.7605 -> 41.76; b = 1.5 and a = 24 from the (1, 36), (4, 121.5) pair; ln2/ln1.25 = 3.106 -> 3.11; 1.25^(1/12) = 1.018769 -> 1.0188 and 0.0188; 40 and 58.773 -> 58.77; 0.25^(1/6) = 0.79370 -> 0.7937 and 6 ln12 / ln4 = 10.755 -> 10.75. All match the key and verify.json. The judge's coverage claim also holds, and it is the important one: I walked every printed Answer line and each has a verify entry - problem 1's two requests, problem 4's exact-and-decimal pair, and the (a)/(b) splits in 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10. Problem 9 is why this sheet avoided the shard's dominant defect: the misconception is exposed by making the student compute 40 and then 58.77 rather than by asking for a sentence, so the diagnostic goal is met entirely inside machine-checkable answers. One defect the judge missed: the Quick Answers bank prints problem 4 as 'e^{0.405465108108164 t}' where the worksheet asks for "the exact value of k as a logarithm". verify.json id 4 declares expected 'exp(t*ln(1.5))', and sympify turns the float 1.5 into a Float so sympy.latex evaluates the logarithm; writing log(Rational(3,2)) renders as e^{t log(3/2)}. The key body is correct ('k = ln 1.5 ~ 0.405'), so this is a banked-form defect, not a mathematical one.

strengths_to_preserve: Problem 9 is the design lesson of this shard. The misconception - reading 1.08 as '8 people a year' - is refuted by asking for two computed increases (40 from t = 0 to 1, then 58.77 from t = 5 to 6) instead of asking for an explanation. Six other cases in this shard were rejected for asking the same kind of question in prose; this one made it verifiable.

Every multi-part problem splits into explicitly enumerated (a)/(b) items each with its own \ansline, and verify.json carries one entry per item. Problems 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10 all follow it, so there is no ambiguity about how many responses the sheet expects.

Problem 10(b) declares answer_unit 'hours' and the sheet prints \answerline{hours}, so the unit is verified data bound to the page rather than decoration - the rendered page 5 shows the unit sitting correctly at the end of the rule.

The models reuse each other: the culture from problem 2 recurs in 3 and 4, the streaming model from 1 recurs in 7 and 8. A student who fits b = 1.5 once then solves for time, converts the base, and rebases to months on the same object.

Problem 8 is a genuinely good rebasing item - b^12 = 1.25 is stated in the stem so the student converts rather than guesses, and it separates the monthly factor 1.0188 from the monthly rate 0.0188, which is the distinction the topic exists to teach.

root_causes.description: render_quick_answers._fmt sympifies a string expected and renders it with sympy.latex. A decimal literal inside a logarithm becomes a sympy Float, so log evaluates numerically and the bank prints a fifteen-digit exponent where the worksheet asked for an exact logarithm.
evidence: scripts/render_quick_answers.py:57-61 - _fmt sympifies string expecteds and returns sympy.latex(...)
worksheet problem 4: 'Give the exact value of k as a logarithm and then as a decimal rounded to three places'

improvements.title: Keep exact logarithms exact in the Quick Answers bank
improvements.proposed_change: Two complementary changes. In SKILL.md, require exact-form expecteds to be written with rationals rather than decimal literals when the stem asks for an exact value - 'exp(t*log(Rational(3,2)))' instead of 'exp(t*ln(1.5))'. In render_quick_answers._fmt, sympify string expecteds with rational=True (or nsimplify floats inside transcendental functions) so a decimal literal does not silently collapse a requested exact form, and warn when a banked entry renders more than six significant digits for a problem whose stem contains 'exact'.
improvements.regression_test: Add a case to tests/test_render_quick_answers.py with expected 'exp(t*ln(1.5))' and assert the rendered bank entry contains a log, not a fifteen-digit float. Fails today (it renders e^{0.405465108108164 t}), passes after the rational-sympify fix.
improvements.expected_impact: The grader's scan column shows the form the worksheet asked for. Applies to every exponential, logarithmic and radical sheet where an exact answer is requested and a decimal parameter appears in the expression.
improvements.risk: rational=True changes how every string expected parses, so an entry that intentionally holds a decimal (an approx target) could shift. Scope the change to _fmt's display path only, leaving verify.py's comparison semantics untouched.

case_summary: The strongest case in my set and a template for the rest of the suite. Ten problems, seventeen checks, every printed Answer line covered, and I could not find an arithmetic error anywhere - the fitted factors, the log-solved times, the rebasing to months and the decay fit all recompute exactly as keyed. What distinguishes it from the six rejected cases is problem 9: it pursues a misconception goal through two computed numbers rather than a requested sentence, so nothing lands outside the verification boundary. The single defect is cosmetic and in the answer key's Quick Answers bank, which prints problem 4 as e^{0.405465108108164 t} because the exact form was encoded with the decimal 1.5 inside the logarithm; the key body prints k = ln 1.5 correctly. Worth fixing because the bank is the surface a grader scans, but it does not touch the verdict.
